short: This family is named after the budding yeast meiotic activator Ndt80, whose DNA-binding domain defines an immunoglobulin-like fold shared by the human proteins MYRF and MYRFL. MYRF, myelin regulatory factor, is the only well-characterized vertebrate member. It is an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein that trimerizes and cleaves itself using a domain related to bacteriophage tailspike proteins; the released N-terminal fragment enters the nucleus and binds DNA. The measured site is the palindromic eight-base TGGTACCA, consistent with binding by a symmetric oligomer. MYRF is required for oligodendrocyte differentiation and for making and maintaining central nervous system myelin, and human MYRF variants cause a cardiac-urogenital syndrome and disorders of sex development.
long:
## The factors

The family is defined by a DNA-binding fold, not by a lineage of related regulators. It takes its
name from Ndt80, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae transcription factor that is activated at pachytene
and turns on roughly 150 middle sporulation genes, including the B-type cyclins, once meiotic
recombination is complete. The crystal structure of the Ndt80 DNA-binding domain showed an
immunoglobulin-like fold, with functional similarities that suggested an evolutionary link to the
p53 family. Human proteins carrying the same Ndt80/PhoG-like domain are MYRF (myelin regulatory
factor, formerly C11orf9 or MRF) and its paralogue MYRFL, which is poorly characterized. MYRF is
unusual for a transcription factor: it is synthesized as a type-2 transmembrane protein in the
endoplasmic reticulum, assembles into a homotrimer, and then cleaves itself through an
autoproteolytic intramolecular chaperone domain that is related to the corresponding domain of
bacteriophage tailspike proteins, the first time that domain was found in a eukaryotic protein.
Cleavage separates the transmembrane C-terminal region from an N-terminal fragment that carries
the DNA-binding domain and a nuclear localization signal. MYRF expression is essentially
restricted to oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system, with some expression in Schwann
cells and other tissues; it is not a broadly expressed factor.

## The motif

All three models in these databases converge on TGGTACCA, an eight-base perfect palindrome, which
is what a symmetric trimeric or dimeric binder would be expected to select: the half-site is TGGT,
read on both strands. The CIS-BP MYRF model and the Vierstra archetype AC0396 are identical to
each other. Chromatin immunoprecipitation of the cleaved N-terminal fragment showed it binding
oligodendrocyte and myelin gene enhancers through a defined consensus, which is consistent with
this palindrome. Information is concentrated in the TGGT/ACCA core; there are no established
spacing rules, and because the site is symmetric, orientation cannot be called from sequence. The
family is not fully coherent here (cohesion 0.73, three motifs). The one discordant model is
HOCOMOCO's MYRFL entry, a long integrative model (GTGCCAGGCNGTGACATCCC) whose best similarity to
any other member of the family is only 0.47, so MYRF and MYRFL should not be assumed to share a
site on the current evidence. The yeast middle sporulation element that Ndt80 reads is a different
sequence again, with a GC-rich 5' half whose pyrimidine-guanine steps are recognized by arginine
side chains through a combination of hydrogen bonding and stacking, and an AT-rich 3' half read
through the minor groove; it is useful as structural background but not as a human motif.

## Where it acts

MYRF sites are found at promoters and, more characteristically, at oligodendrocyte-specific distal
enhancers of myelin genes, including MBP, PLP1, MAG and CNP. Enhancer mapping at the Plp1 locus
identified two oligodendrocyte-specific enhancers, both acted on by MYRF, whose contacts with the
gene are among the strongest in that cell type. MYRF works with SOX10 at many of these elements,
so a MYRF match near a SOX10 dimer site in oligodendrocyte-accessible chromatin is a much stronger
signal than the match alone. As an eight-base fixed palindrome, TGGTACCA is expected by chance on
the order of tens of thousands of times in a human genome, most of them in closed chromatin and in
cell types where MYRF is absent.

## Biology and disease

Mice lacking Myrf in the oligodendrocyte lineage fail to myelinate the central nervous system, and
inducible deletion in adults causes loss of myelin and of mature oligodendrocyte identity, so MYRF
is required for maintenance as well as for differentiation. In humans, de novo MYRF variants cause
a syndrome of congenital cardiac and urogenital anomalies, often with congenital diaphragmatic
hernia, and MYRF haploinsufficiency has been reported in both 46,XY and 46,XX disorders of sex
development. The link between a myelin regulator and cardiac and gonadal development is not
explained by the oligodendrocyte role, and likely reflects earlier developmental expression.

## Reading a hit

The palindrome is short and fully specified, so chance matches are common and the sequence alone
carries no cell-type information. A MYRF match matters only in a cell that expresses MYRF, which
in practice means the oligodendrocyte lineage; elsewhere the same eight bases are inert. Do not
assume that a match to the MYRFL model is equivalent to a MYRF site: that model is discordant with
the MYRF palindrome in these data. Because MYRF requires autoproteolytic release to reach the
nucleus, the presence of MYRF protein in a tissue does not establish that its DNA-binding fragment
is present, which is an unusual extra step between motif and function. Treat the yeast Ndt80 MSE
as a separate element that shares only the fold.
caveats: Only three motifs and two proteins sit under this key, and one of them disagrees with the other two: the HOCOMOCO MYRFL model matches the MYRF palindrome at only 0.47, so MYRF and MYRFL cannot be assumed interchangeable. TGGTACCA is eight fixed bases and a perfect palindrome, so chance matches number in the tens of thousands per genome and orientation is undefined. The site is only interpretable in cells expressing MYRF, essentially the oligodendrocyte lineage. MYRF also needs autoproteolytic cleavage before its DNA-binding fragment reaches the nucleus, so protein presence does not imply DNA binding. The yeast Ndt80 MSE shares the fold but not the sequence.
